intro.html: Writers about science, health and history need exact words for harm: harm that is quick or slow, open or hidden, to the body or to a plan. They also need a few words for the opposite, the things that do us good.

Harmful in general: detrimental, deleterious. Poison and fumes: toxic, noxious. Hidden or slow harm: pernicious, insidious. Fierce harm: virulent. Unfriendly: inimical. Good for you: salutary (a helpful effect), salubrious (healthful).
Two Latin roots help: salus means health (salutary, salubrious), and amicus means friend, so inimical (in- + amicus) means unfriendly.

words.ex: Staying up all night is {detrimental} to your grades.
words.ctx: The new parking lot proved {detrimental} to the pond: oil washed off the pavement with every rain, and within two years the frogs had disappeared.
words.etym: From Latin detrimentum, “loss, damage,” from deterere (to rub away, to wear down).

mn.cue: de-TRIM-ental: too much TRIM does HARM
mn.text: Pip trims Grandpa’s little bush, then trims some more, and more, until only a bare stick is left; all that trimming is {detrimental} to the bush.

scene.alt: A boy proudly holds a saw beside a stump that used to be a bush while his grandfather gasps.

words.ex: Some common garden flowers are {toxic} to cats.
words.ctx: The old paint in the house was {toxic}: it contained lead, which can make children seriously ill if they swallow even tiny chips.
words.etym: From Late Latin toxicus, from Greek toxikon, poison smeared on arrows (from toxon, a bow).
words.note: Today toxic is also used for anything that harms people slowly, like a toxic friendship.

mn.text: The bottle under the sink has a big warning label and a skull on it; what is inside is {toxic}, so the cat backs away.

scene.alt: A cat backs away from a green poison bottle as a woman warns that it is not for pets.

words.def: harmful, especially to health; also, very unpleasant
words.ex: The {noxious} fumes from the burning tires drove everyone indoors.
words.ctx: Unlike the harmless steam from the kettle, the gas leaking from the old furnace was {noxious}, and the family had to leave the house until it was repaired.
words.note: Noxious fumes harm you; obnoxious people only annoy you.

mn.cue: KNOCKS-ious: fumes that KNOCK you back
mn.text: The old truck coughs out a black cloud so foul that it nearly knocks the jogger off his feet; its fumes are {noxious}.

scene.alt: A jogger staggers back from the thick black exhaust pouring from an old car.

words.def: causing great harm, often slowly or in a way that is hard to see
words.ex: Gossip can have a {pernicious} effect on a friendship.
words.ctx: The habit seemed harmless at first, a few minutes of games before homework, but it proved {pernicious}, quietly eating up whole evenings until her grades began to slip.
words.etym: From Latin perniciosus, “ruinous,” from pernicies (ruin, destruction).

mn.text: The pretty pink flowers spreading through Lin’s garden look nice, but week by week they choke out every bean and carrot; the weed is {pernicious}.

scene.alt: Pretty weeds have spread across a garden, crowding out the vegetables, while the gardener frowns.

words.def: harmful, often in a way that is not obvious at first
words.ex: Too much sun can have {deleterious} effects on your skin.
words.ctx: The chemical seemed safe in short tests, but over the years it proved {deleterious}, slowly weakening the shells of the birds whose food it touched.
words.etym: From Greek deleterios, “harmful,” from deleisthai (to hurt).

mn.text: A sneaky computer bug deletes one of Sami’s files every night, until his whole science project is nearly gone; the bug is {deleterious}.

scene.alt: A boy panics as a sneaky bug on his desk deletes the files on his laptop.

words.ex: Rust is {insidious}: it eats away at a bridge long before anyone sees the damage.
words.ctx: The rumor was {insidious}; no one noticed it spreading from table to table until, weeks later, half the class had stopped speaking to Dev.
words.etym: From Latin insidiosus, “cunning,” from insidiae (an ambush), from insidere (to sit in, to lie in wait).

mn.text: A tiny leak drips inside the wall for months where no one can see it, until the ceiling sags; the damage is {insidious}.

scene.alt: Water drips from a hidden leak in the ceiling into a bucket as a grandmother looks up in shock.

words.def: extremely harmful or severe; also, bitterly hostile
words.ex: A {virulent} flu swept through the school, closing it for a week.
words.ctx: The critic’s review was {virulent}: instead of simply disliking the play, she attacked the actors, the director and even the audience for clapping.
words.etym: From Latin virulentus, “full of poison,” from virus (poison, venom).
words.note: Also said VEER-uh-lunt, without the y sound.

mn.cue: VIRUS-lent: a VIRUS at full strength
mn.text: This flu spreads so fast and hits so hard that by Friday only one student is left in the classroom; it is {virulent}.

scene.alt: A worried teacher stands in a nearly empty classroom where one sick boy sneezes.

words.def: harmful or unfriendly, like an enemy
words.ex: Cold, salty air is {inimical} to most tropical plants.
words.ctx: The desert’s scorching days and freezing nights are {inimical} to most living things, yet the tough little cactus thrives there.
words.etym: From Late Latin inimicalis, from Latin inimicus (enemy): in- (not) + amicus (friend).

mn.cue: IN-IMIC: NOT AMICable, NOT a friend
mn.text: The snowman who wandered into the desert finds the blazing sun no friend at all; the heat is {inimical} to him.

scene.alt: A snowman melts into a puddle under the blazing desert sun.

words.def: having a good effect, often after a hard lesson
words.ex: Losing the first game had a {salutary} effect on the team: they practiced twice as hard.
words.ctx: Though the low grade stung, it proved {salutary}; Kai began studying every night and finished the year near the top of his class.
words.etym: From Latin salutaris, “healthful,” from salus (health, safety).
words.note: Salutary has nothing to do with saluting today, though both go back to salus: a salute was once a wish for someone’s good health.

mn.text: After missing the bus once, Dev sets an alarm every night and never misses it again; he salutes the lesson, which was {salutary}.

scene.alt: A teen proudly salutes his alarm clock after learning not to miss the bus.

words.ex: The village was known for its {salubrious} climate, with clean air and mild summers.
words.ctx: After years in the smoky city, Grandma moved to a {salubrious} seaside town, where she walked the beach every morning and slept better than she had in decades.
words.etym: From Latin salubris, “healthful,” related to salus (health).

mn.text: Every day Nana Lou eats a fresh salad in the cool sea breeze; her seaside town is {salubrious}.

scene.alt: A grandmother in a straw hat happily eats a salad in the sea breeze.

head: word
kind of harm (or good)
rows: harmful in general (deleterious often not obvious at first)
slow, hidden harm (insidious creeps in secretly)
fierce and severe (a virulent disease, virulent words)
has a good effect, often a hard lesson
after.cap: Ten words for what harms and what helps.

after.html: Noxious fumes harm you; an obnoxious person only annoys you. And salutary (good for you) has nothing to do with saluting today.

items.q: “The scare had a salutary effect: from then on, the hikers always carried a map.” Salutary means…
items.why: A salutary effect is a good one, often after a hard lesson. It has nothing to do with saluting.

items.q: Which word describes harmful fumes, not an annoying person?
items.why: Noxious means harmful to health. Obnoxious means very annoying.

items.q: Inimical is built from in- (not) and the Latin amicus, which means…
items.why: amicus means friend (as in amicable): inimical means unfriendly, harmful.

items.q: Which word best describes harm that spreads slowly and secretly, like a hidden leak?
items.why: Insidious harm creeps in unnoticed; its Latin root means an ambush.
